blocks.text: 2.2.2 Getter and Setter Methods in Java

A guest asks the front desk to move a stay from 10–12 March to 20–22 March. The app calls `setCheckIn`, then `setCheckOut`, and the move is refused: `check-in 2026-03-20 is not before check-out 2026-03-12`. In the same order, moving a stay earlier works. Both setters validate.
A Setter Can Check Its Own Value, Not a Rule That Spans Two Fields
`Stay` keeps check-in before check-out. Each setter checks its new value against the other field; `reschedule` takes both:
Before reading on: for a move later, which order of the two setters works? For a move earlier?

later, in then out: check-in 2026-03-20 is not before check-out 2026-03-12, stay is 2026-03-10..2026-03-12
later, out then in: 2026-03-20..2026-03-22
earlier, out then in: check-out 2026-03-03 is not after check-in 2026-03-10, stay is 2026-03-10..2026-03-12
reschedule later: 2026-03-20..2026-03-22
reschedule earlier: 2026-03-01..2026-03-03

A setter compares its value with the fields as they are now, and in the middle of a two-step change one of them still holds the old date. The order that works depends on the direction of the move, so a caller that learns "out first" breaks the other way. A rule over two fields belongs in one method that receives both values.

That method checks every argument before it assigns any field. A version that assigns `checkIn` first and then throws leaves the stay as `2026-03-20..2026-03-12`, a state no setter would have accepted.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Getter That Returns a Date or an Array Hands Out the Field
Unit 1.3.2 showed a getter that returns its internal list. `java.util.Date` and arrays leak the same way, and `private final` only stops reassignment. A signed contract has these getters:

Contract c = new Contract(new Date(1_767_225_600_000L), "ana", "bo");
c.getSignedAt().setTime(0);                 // a report "normalises" the date it was given
c.getApprovers()[1] = "mallory";            // a caller edits the array it got back
c.approverList().set(0, "eve");             // Arrays.asList is a view of the array

signed:  2026-01-01T00:00:00Z [ana, bo]
after:   1970-01-01T00:00:00Z [ana, mallory]
asList:  1970-01-01T00:00:00Z [eve, mallory]

The contract prints its date with `toInstant()`. It copied both arguments in its constructor (unit 1.3.3), and its getters still handed out the fields. `Arrays.asList` copies nothing: its `set` writes into the array. Return `new Date(signedAt.getTime())` and `approvers.clone()`, or store an `Instant` and a `List.of(...)` copy, which no caller can change, and return them as they are.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Tools Find Properties by Method Name, and isX Works Only for a Primitive boolean
JavaBeans tools, including the JDK's `java.beans.Introspector`, look for methods named `getX`, `isX` and `setX`, not for fields. A class `Flags` has these accessors:
`Introspector.getBeanInfo(type, Object.class)`, which leaves out `getClass()`, on `Flags` and on `record Endpoint(String host, int port)`:

Flags:
  URL      read=getURL()   write=setURL()
  active   read=isActive() write=setActive()
  area     read=getArea()  write=-
  enabled  read=-          write=setEnabled()
  port     read=getPort()  write=-
Endpoint:

`is` names a getter only when it returns a primitive `boolean`, so `enabled` can be written and never read. A setter must return `void`: the fluent `setPort` is invisible, and a binder built on the introspector leaves every port at its default. `getArea()` has no field behind it and is still a read-only property. `getURL` gives the property `URL`, not `url`: a name whose first two letters are capitals keeps its case. A record's accessors have no prefix, so the introspector finds no property in `Endpoint`.
**Libraries differ.** Jackson, Spring and others apply their own versions of these rules. Check the one you bind with.
A Record's Accessor Is name(), and Overriding It Doesn't Change equals
A record's accessor may be declared explicitly, as long as it is `public` with the component's type. This one normalises a tag:
Two tags, `new Tag("Java")` and `new Tag(" java ")`:

names:  java / java
equals: false, toString: Tag[name=Java] / Tag[name= java ]
set size: 2
pattern sees: [java]
copy equals original: false

The generated `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` read the fields, not the accessors, so two tags that report the same name are two entries in a set. A record pattern `Tag(String n)` calls the accessor and sees `java`. `new Tag(b.name())` is not equal to `b`, which breaks the contract in `Record.equals`'s javadoc: a record rebuilt from its accessors must equal the original.
Normalise in the compact constructor instead, so the field holds the value every method sees:
compact: true, NormalTag[name=java] / NormalTag[name=java]

Summary

items: **A setter checks one value against the current state.** A rule spanning two fields needs one method that validates both arguments, then assigns.
**A getter that returns a `Date` or an array hands out the field.** Return a copy, or store an immutable type.
**Tools find properties by method name.** `isX` only for `boolean`, setters return `void`, and a record's accessors have no prefix.
**A record's `equals` and `toString` read fields, not accessors.** Normalise in the compact constructor.

blocks.text: **Record accessors:** an explicit accessor must be `public` and return the component's type; `javac` rejects `String code()` without `public`.
Challenges

items: A `Meeting` has `start`, `end` and `room`, and a move must keep the room free. Which method owns that check, and what does a caller that only changes the room call?
Your JSON library binds a `Boolean isArchived()`. Find out whether it reads it, and what it writes for `null`.
A record holds a `List<String>`. Do you copy it in the compact constructor, in the accessor, or both, and what does each choice do to `equals`?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why Records Didn't Adopt getX

A record's state is its components: the canonical constructor takes them, the accessors return them under the same names, and `new R(r.a(), r.b())` rebuilds it. The JavaBeans prefix was a convention for tools to discover properties to read and write, and a record has nothing to write. The cost falls on tools built on that convention: a record bound by one needs a `getHost()` added by hand.
